messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir, a 38-year-old hairdresser who had built a loyal clientele over fifteen years at the same salon in Dearborn, Michigan, could trace the exact moment his life split in two. It was a Tuesday afternoon, three years ago, when a routine physical for a minor shoulder strain turned catastrophic. The doctor, a man Amir had seen twice before, had pulled up a CT scan on the monitor and said, in a voice so flat it seemed rehearsed, that there was a mass on his pancreas. The word "malignant" came next. Amir remembered the fluorescent hum of the lights, the antiseptic sting in the air, and the way his own breath suddenly smelled wrong to him—metallic, sour, like something inside him was already rotting. He remembered the exact pressure of the cold stethoscope disk against his sternum as the doctor listened to his heart, and how that pressure, that listening, had felt like a verdict being delivered to every cell in his body.

What followed was eight months of surgeries and chemotherapy, and Amir survived. The cancer went into remission. But his body had not forgiven him. Now, years later, the smell of antiseptic wipes in the salon—the kind he used to clean his clippers without a second thought—would hit him like a wave, and suddenly he could taste that copper-sour smell from the exam room again, his mouth filling with a phantom metallic saliva. When he woke from nightmares, which he did most nights now, he would lie perfectly still in the dark, his hand pressed to his abdomen, certain he could feel the exact ache of the surgical incision, the ghost of the drain tube pulling at his skin. The worst moments were the ones he could not explain to anyone: he would be standing over a client, chatting about the weather, and a wave of pure terror would crash through him—cold, electric, wordless—with no image attached, no memory, just the full, suffocating feeling of being told he was going to die. He had come to believe that these episodes proved something terrible about himself. His body kept reacting as if the cancer were still there, as if danger were still present, and there was no logical reason for it. That, to Amir, meant he was going crazy. His own nervous system had become a traitor, and he could not trust a single sensation it sent him.

He had started declining medical care. A routine blood test last spring sent him into a spiral so severe he had to close the salon for two days. He had sat in the waiting room, his skin prickling with heat, his heart slamming against his ribs, and when the phlebotomist touched his arm he had flinched so violently he knocked over a tray of vials. He had not gone back for the results. The thought of another examination, another cold probe, another doctor’s pause before speaking, was not just frightening—it was unendurable. At work, he had become brittle. The salon was full of mirrors, and sometimes, catching his own reflection in a certain light, he would see the gaunt, bald man from the hospital photos and his hands would start to shake. He had learned to angle his chair away from the glass. He had also learned to avoid the salon’s back room, where a framed photo from his salon’s ten-year anniversary party still hung—a picture of himself, healthy and smiling, that now felt like a photograph of a dead man.

He was single, and he had stopped dating entirely. The thought of someone touching his torso, of a lover’s hand brushing the scar tissue that ran from his sternum to his navel, made his throat close. He was certain no one could understand what it felt like to live in a body that had turned into an enemy, a body that could not be trusted not to betray him again. What brought Amir to therapy, finally, was not the terror itself but the exhaustion. He had woken up one morning after a nightmare, his sheets soaked with sweat, his hand already pressing into his abdomen, and he had realized he could not remember what it felt like to wake up without that gesture. He was tired of being afraid of his own pulse. He was tired of the smell of rubbing alcohol ruining his days. He did not know if talking could fix a body that had taught him it could kill him, but he was desperate enough to hope that it might.
